input.draft:
Let a potential triple be any three consecutive cells in one row or column. A terminal collection of removed blocks must meet every potential triple.

For n≥3 there are
\[
2n(n-2)
\]
potential triples. A horizontal removed block meets at most five horizontal potential triples: their starting positions differ from the block's starting position by at most 2. Its three cells meet at most three vertical triples each, hence at most nine vertical triples. Thus it meets at most 14 potential triples. The same holds for a vertical block. Consequently every terminal collection of k blocks satisfies
\[
14k\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
so
\[
b(n)\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
For n=1,2 this inequality also holds, since b(n)=0. Thus we may take c=2/7.

For the upper bound, first define a periodic packing of the infinite square lattice. In row r, place horizontal blocks beginning at every column s satisfying
\[
r+s\equiv0\pmod 5.
\]
The blocks in each row are separated by two cells and are therefore disjoint. Their union is exactly
\[
D=\{(r,q):r+q\pmod5\in\{0,1,2\}\}.
\]
Every horizontal triple meets D, because among three consecutive residues modulo 5 at least one belongs to \(\{0,1,2\}\). The same argument, with the row coordinate varying, shows that every vertical triple meets D.

Now suppose n≥6 and restrict this infinite construction to rows and columns 1 through n. Retain every periodic block lying entirely within the board. In each row, if a periodic block intersects the left edge without being contained in the board, add the horizontal block in columns 1,2,3. Likewise, if a periodic block intersects the right edge without being contained, add the block in columns n-2,n-1,n.

These added blocks are disjoint from the retained blocks. Indeed, a block crossing the left edge starts at -1 or 0, so the next periodic block starts at 4 or 5; the right-edge case is symmetric. The two added boundary blocks are disjoint because n≥6. Moreover, every cell of D lying in the board is removed: its infinite periodic block is either retained or its portion inside the board is covered by one of the added boundary blocks. Hence every horizontal or vertical triple in the board is hit, so no further block can be removed.

In each row there are at most \(n/5+1\) retained periodic blocks and at most two added boundary blocks. Therefore the total number used is at most
\[
n\left(\frac n5+3\right)=\frac15n^2+3n.
\]
For 1≤n≤5, greedily removing blocks until none remains uses at most \(n^2/3\) blocks, which is at most \(n^2/5+3n\). Thus the upper bound holds for every positive integer n with d=3.

Therefore
\[
\frac17n^2-\frac27n\le b(n)\le\frac15n^2+3n
\]
for all positive integers n, proving the theorem.

feedback.reason: The proof is valid. Terminality is correctly translated into hitting every length-three row or column segment. Each removed block intersects at most 14 such segments, giving the stated lower bound. The periodic horizontal packing is disjoint, its occupied set meets every horizontal and vertical triple, and the boundary modifications remain disjoint while covering all occupied lattice cells inside the board. The block count yields the upper bound, and the small cases are adequately handled.

problem.proof_text:
Proof.  We think of the final “blocked’’ configuration as the result of tearing out \(b(n)\) disjoint 3-stamp blocks (each block either 3 in a row or 3 in a column) so that no further 3-stamp block remains.  Call any three consecutive positions in a row or in a column a “potential triple.’’  There are in all  
\[
H \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{horizontal triples,}
\qquad
V \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{vertical triples,}
\]
and hence 
\[
T \;=\;H+V \;=\;2\,n\,(n-2)
\]
potential triples that must each be “hit’’ (i.e.\ each must lose at least one stamp) by our removed blocks.

1.  Lower bound \(b(n)\ge \tfrac1{7}n^2-cn\).  
 
Fix any one of the \(b(n)\) removed blocks.  If it is a horizontal block occupying cells \((i,j),(i,j+1),(i,j+2)\), then it “hits’’ (i.e.\ destroys at least one cell of) at most
  •  all horizontal triples that include one of those three cells;  in a row of length \(n\), each interior cell lies in 3 horizontal triples and each end‐cell in 1 or 2, and one checks easily that the three consecutive cells \((i,j),(i,j+1),(i,j+2)\) together lie in at most 5 distinct horizontal triples;  
  •  all vertical triples that include one of those three cells;  each of the three removed stamps lies in at most 3 vertical triples, so altogether at most \(3\times3=9\) vertical triples.  
Hence that one horizontal block can destroy at most \(5+9=14\) of the \(T\) potential triples.  Likewise any vertical block destroys at most \(14\) potential triples.  

Since in the final configuration every one of the \(T=2n(n-2)\) potential triples must be destroyed by at least one of the removed blocks, and since each block can destroy at most \(14\) triples, we get the inequality
\[
14\,b(n)\;\ge\;2\,n(n-2)\;=\;2n^2-4n,
\]
i.e.
\[
b(n)\;\ge\;\frac{2n^2-4n}{14}
\;=\;\frac1{7}\,n^2-\frac{2}{7}\,n.
\]
Thus the stated lower bound holds with \(c=\tfrac{2}{7}\).

2.  Upper bound \(b(n)\le \tfrac1{5}n^2+dn\).

We give an explicit “tiling’’ construction with density \(1/5\), up to an \(O(n)\) boundary correction.  Assume for simplicity that \(n\) is a multiple of 5; the leftover strip of width \(<5\) on the right and top can then be handled by at most \(O(n)\) extra blocks without changing the leading term.

Partition the \(n\times n\) grid into \(\tfrac n5\times\tfrac n5\) little \(5\times5\) macrosquares.  In each \(5\times5\) macro with local coordinates \((r,c)\), \(1\le r,c\le5\), remove exactly the following 5 blocks (each of size 3):

  A)  A horizontal block in row \(r=2\), columns \(c=1,2,3\).

  B)  A horizontal block in row \(r=4\), columns \(c=3,4,5\).

  C)  A vertical block in column \(c=2\), rows \(r=3,4,5\).

  D)  A vertical block in column \(c=4\), rows \(r=1,2,3\).

  E)  A horizontal block in row \(r=5\), columns \(c=2,3,4\).

One checks by an easy (though a bit tedious) case‐by‐case verification that in this repeated pattern every horizontal triple of three consecutive stamps in any row will contain at least one removed stamp (from one of the above horizontal blocks in its macro or in an adjacent macro), and similarly every vertical triple of three consecutive stamps in any column meets one of the vertical blocks C) or D).  Thus after tearing out these \(5\) blocks in each \(5\times5\) cell there is no triple left anywhere in the \(n\times n\) square.

Since there are \(\tfrac n5\) macros in each direction, the total number of blocks used is
\[
5\;\times\;\Bigl(\frac n5\Bigr)^2
\;=\;\frac15\,n^2.
\]
Adding the \(O(n)\) extra blocks needed to cover the final partial strips (of width \(<5\)) along the top and right edges gives
\[
b(n)\;\le\;\frac15\,n^2 \;+\;O(n).
\]
Hence the upper bound holds with some constant \(d\).

Combining (1) and (2) completes the proof: for all \(n>0\),
\[
\frac1{7}\,n^2-\frac{2}{7}n\;\le\;b(n)\;\le\;\frac1{5}\,n^2+d\,n,
\]
as required.  ∎
problem.theorem:
I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).

rule_candidates.conclusion: G/N is a group and coset multiplication is well-defined.
conditions: N is a subgroup of G
rule_candidates.name: Quotient group criterion
rule_candidates.statement: If N is a normal subgroup of G, then the set of left cosets G/N forms a group under (aN)(bN) = abN.

rule_candidates.conclusion: R/I is a ring and coset operations are well-defined.
conditions: I is a two-sided ideal of R
rule_candidates.name: Quotient ring criterion
rule_candidates.statement: If I is a two-sided ideal of a ring R, then R/I is a quotient ring with operations defined on cosets.

conditions: ker(phi) is the kernel of phi
rule_candidates.name: First isomorphism theorem for groups
rule_candidates.statement: If phi: G -> H is a group homomorphism, then G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).
